name: Narcolepsy
summary: Narcolepsy is a chronic central disorder of hypersomnolence with excessive daytime sleepiness, with or without cataplexy (type 1 reflects orexin/hypocretin loss). FDA-labeled options include wake-promoting agents (modafinil, armodafinil, solriamfetol, pitolisant), oxybates for EDS and cataplexy (REMS-restricted), older stimulants, and, since August 2026, the first orexin-2 receptor agonist, oveporexton, for narcolepsy type 1 in adults.
plainSummary: Narcolepsy is a brain condition that causes strong sleepiness during the day. Some people also have sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotions such as laughter (cataplexy). Several medicines can improve alertness and reduce these attacks.

approved.indication: To improve wakefulness in adult patients with excessive sleepiness associated with narcolepsy.

dosing.start: 200 mg once daily in the morning
dosing.max: 400 mg/day (studied, but no consistent added benefit over 200 mg)
dosing.notes: Severe hepatic impairment: half the usual dose. Consider lower doses in geriatric patients. Reduces effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives (CYP3A4 induction).

contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to modafinil or armodafinil
approved.plainSummary: Modafinil helps people with narcolepsy stay awake during the day. Rarely it can cause serious rash or allergic reactions.

approved.indication: To improve wakefulness in adult patients with excessive daytime sleepiness associated with narcolepsy.

dosing.notes: May double dose at intervals of at least 3 days. Avoid within 9 hours of bedtime. Control blood pressure before starting. Moderate renal impairment: start 37.5 mg, max 75 mg; severe: 37.5 mg max; ESRD: not recommended.

approved.plainSummary: Solriamfetol helps adults with narcolepsy stay awake during the day. It can raise blood pressure and heart rate.

approved.indication: Treatment of excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) in patients 6 years of age and older with narcolepsy.

population.ages: Adults and pediatric patients 6 years and older

dosing.start: Adults: 8.9 mg once daily on waking (week 1). Pediatric: 4.45 mg once daily (week 1)
dosing.target: Adults: 17.8–35.6 mg once daily. Pediatric: 17.8 mg (<40 kg) or up to 35.6 mg (≥40 kg)
dosing.notes: Weekly titration. Consider CYP2D6 genotyping: poor metabolizers max 17.8 mg (adults). Moderate hepatic impairment or eGFR <60: lower maximum (adults 17.8 mg). ESRD: not recommended. Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors or strong CYP3A4 inducers require adjustment. May reduce hormonal contraceptive effectiveness; QT prolongation caution.

contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to pitolisant or formulation components
approved.plainSummary: Pitolisant boosts histamine, a brain chemical that promotes wakefulness, to help with daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy. It is not a controlled substance.

verified.note: Checked against the current SPL (effective February 2026). Adult EDS approved 2019; per news reports, the pediatric (6 years and older) EDS extension was approved June 2024.

approved.indication: Treatment of cataplexy in patients 6 years of age and older with narcolepsy.

population.ages: Adults and pediatric patients 6 years and older

dosing.start: Adults: 8.9 mg once daily on waking (week 1). Pediatric: 4.45 mg once daily (week 1)
dosing.target: Adults: 17.8–35.6 mg once daily. Pediatric: 17.8 mg (<40 kg) or up to 35.6 mg (≥40 kg)
dosing.notes: Same titration and dose limits as for EDS (CYP2D6 poor metabolizers, hepatic and renal impairment).

contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to pitolisant or formulation components
approved.plainSummary: Pitolisant also reduces cataplexy, the sudden muscle weakness some people with narcolepsy have, in adults and children 6 and older.

verified.note: Adult cataplexy approved 2020. The pediatric cataplexy extension (6 years and older) was approved February 17, 2026 (AASM/NeurologyLive reports); the current label reflects it.

approved.indication: Treatment of excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) in patients 7 years of age and older with narcolepsy.

population.ages: Adults and pediatric patients 7 years and older

dosing.start: Adults: 4.5 g/night divided into 2 doses (bedtime and 2.5–4 hours later)
dosing.max: 9 g/night (pediatric: weight-based, e.g., 9 g/night if ≥45 kg)
dosing.notes: Titrate by 1.5 g/night weekly. Pediatric starting doses and maximums are weight-based (insufficient data under 20 kg). Take at least 2 hours after eating, in bed. Hepatic impairment: start at half dose. High sodium load. Avoid with valproate unless dose adjusted.

boxedWarnings: CNS depression, including respiratory depression and obtundation
Abuse and misuse (GHB); available only through a restricted REMS program
approved.rems: XYWAV and XYREM REMS (generic sodium oxybate products are also REMS-restricted; check the individual label)
approved.plainSummary: Sodium oxybate is a liquid taken at bedtime and again during the night. It improves nighttime sleep and reduces daytime sleepiness. It is strictly controlled because it can slow breathing and can be misused.

verified.note: Checked against the Xyrem SPL (effective July 2025). Generic sodium oxybate oral solutions (e.g., Hikma, Amneal) are listed on DailyMed. Adult EDS approved 2005 (cataplexy 2002); the pediatric extension was approved in 2018. Approval years are from FDA approval history and were not re-checked.

approved.indication: Narcolepsy (listed with ADHD in section 1). Long-acting ADHD-only products such as Concerta and Ritalin LA are not labeled for narcolepsy.

population.ages: No age range given for narcolepsy; label dosing covers adults and pediatric patients 6 years and older

dosing.start: Adults: divided doses 2–3 times daily, 30–45 minutes before meals. Pediatric (6+): 5 mg twice daily
dosing.notes: Increase pediatric dose by 5–10 mg weekly. Take last dose before 6 p.m. if insomnia occurs. ER tablets (10 mg, 20 mg; about 8-hour duration) may replace IR once titrated. Screen for cardiac disease before starting.

contraindications: MAOI use currently or within 14 days
approved.plainSummary: Methylphenidate is a stimulant that can help people with narcolepsy stay awake. It can be misused and may raise heart rate and blood pressure.

verified.note: Ritalin (Sandoz, effective February 2025), Methylin oral solution, Metadate ER, and generic methylphenidate ER 10/20 mg tablets (SpecGx, setid ed004cf0-eb23-43d2-96dc-20c4ad63824f) all list narcolepsy. Approval year for the narcolepsy indication predates modern records and is not confirmed.

approved.indication: Treatment of narcolepsy type 1 (narcolepsy with cataplexy) in adult patients.

dosing.start: 1 mg after awakening + 1 mg 3–5 hours later, OR 2 mg after awakening + 2 mg 3–5 hours later
dosing.notes: Swallow whole at about the same time each day, with or without food. Moderate CYP3A inhibitors: 0.5 mg twice (1 mg/day max). Avoid strong or moderate CYP3A inducers. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) and severe renal impairment on dialysis. Insomnia (55–60% in trials), urinary frequency or urgency, and CPK elevations are the key warnings.

approved.plainSummary: Oveporexton is the first medicine that replaces the missing orexin signal in narcolepsy type 1. It is a pill taken twice in the morning and early afternoon, and it can cause trouble sleeping and frequent urination.

source.label: FDA label: Orzeyful (oveporexton) prescribing information, August 2026 (Drugs@FDA)

verified.note: FDA approved August 5, 2026 (NDA 220860). Checked against the FDA label PDF; it is not yet on DailyMed. The label says 'controlled substance schedule pending', so controlledSubstance is null until DEA scheduling (expected around November 2026). Takeda plans to launch after scheduling, so the drug may not be commercially available yet.

offLabel.notes: Strong recommendation for cataplexy in adults in the 2021 European (EAN/ESRS/EU-NN) guideline, based mainly on clinical experience and limited trial data. It is not FDA-labeled for narcolepsy. Cautions: abrupt discontinuation can cause severe rebound cataplexy (status cataplecticus); also hypertension and the antidepressant boxed warning for suicidality in young people.

references.label: Bassetti CLA et al. European guideline and expert statements on the management of narcolepsy in adults and children. Eur J Neurol 2021

offLabel.notes: Strong recommendation for adult cataplexy in the 2021 European guideline. Cautions: anticholinergic effects, orthostasis, weight gain, sexual dysfunction, lowered seizure threshold, cardiac conduction effects, and rebound cataplexy on abrupt withdrawal.

references.label: Bassetti CLA et al. European guideline on the management of narcolepsy. Eur J Neurol 2021
Vignatelli L et al. Antidepressant drugs for narcolepsy. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2008

offLabel.notes: Used for cataplexy based on small studies and clinical experience; a Cochrane review found insufficient high-quality evidence for antidepressants in narcolepsy. Cautions: rebound cataplexy on abrupt stop, possible worsening of REM sleep behavior symptoms, and the antidepressant boxed warning in young people.

references.label: Vignatelli L et al. Antidepressant drugs for narcolepsy. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2008

offLabel.use: Excessive daytime sleepiness in children with narcolepsy
offLabel.notes: FDA-labeled only for adults. The AASM 2021 guideline gives a conditional recommendation for modafinil in pediatric narcolepsy. Cautions: serious rash including Stevens-Johnson syndrome (higher concern in children), psychiatric symptoms, and reduced hormonal contraceptive efficacy.

references.label: Maski K et al. Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: AASM clinical practice guideline. J Clin Sleep Med 2021
